reviewNotes: No person has reviewed this file.

Crux is 7.3, not 7.2. IM's lesson narrative calls the across-the-columns idea the lesson's new insight, and goal 3 and learning target 2 are about it. 7.2 sets it up (equivalent ratios have the same unit rate); 7.4 is optional practice.
Testable object: the strategy sentence 7.3 asks for (“explain the strategy you used”). Question 2 of 7.3 tests it by asking pairs to reuse the strategy on the burrito table.

IM's own moments used: the “14 per 2” misconception in 7.2, the student for whom the table's structure “may not be apparent” in 7.3, the 1-hour-row strategy and the share order in 7.3's narrative and synthesis.
Premo's moments: the hands-up breakdown of Think Pair Share (from IM's routine definition), the 16 r 4 remainder, the language moment and its by-level moves, the warm-up and applesauce moments.
IM's English-learner support for 7.2 quotes the question as “buy \(b\) burritos for 4 dollars”; the task says “\(c\) dollars”. Looks like a typo in IM. Not repeated here.
Student responses and the cool-down were transcribed from the Teacher Guide page images by a model, not checked by a person.

Revised 2026-10-23 after persona review: the 1-hour row is now treated the same way in watchFor, m3 and m5 (a valid strategy; ask the pair to be ready to share first, as IM says, instead of steering them to the 6); m3's evidence now includes IM's “consider asking them to share first”; the “16 r 4 hours” pattern is re-typed from error to almost and m7 calls it unfinished, not wrong; m6 and cruxLanguage ask every level the same question, across the table and back (multiply and divide by 6), with only the way in differing, and the extra “say why” for Levels 5–6 is gone; m1's say line no longer starts with a quoted phrase; home language is offered at every level; jargon (display tour, synthesis, share, MLR name in beforeClass) replaced with plain words; a 7.3 time note added to cuts, since posters and a walk-around don't fit IM's 10 minutes; beforeClass trimmed to three short tasks, including the answer key.
cruxWhy: 7.3 is where the lesson's new idea is first used: the unit rate is the factor that takes you from one column to the other. IM's lesson narrative calls this the lesson's new insight, and its goals and second learning target are about it. IM’s language support for the lesson sits in 7.3’s closing class discussion.

object.name: the strategy sentence
object.what: The sentence each pair writes under the bracelet table saying how they filled it. Question 2 tests it: use the same strategy on the burrito table.

goal: Students use the unit rate to move across a table, multiplying or dividing by it, and say why equivalent ratios share one unit rate.
rigorCheck: Does every pair still fill the bracelet table, write the strategy sentence, and hear the strategies in IM’s order, the 1-hour row first?

watchFor.7.1: A group stops at one reason and calls it the answer.
watchFor.7.2: The unit price column says “14 per 2”, not 7.
watchFor.7.3: A pair builds a 1-hour row first. Ask them to be ready to share it first.
watchFor.7.4: Doubling 4 pounds to 8, then stuck at 7.

moments.see: The unit price column reads “14 per 2” and “28 per 4.”
moments.means: They kept the ratio. The column asks what one burrito costs.
moments.say: Per burrito means for one burrito. What does one cost?
moments.evidence: Students may not realize that the third column asks for dollars per 1 burrito and instead write 14 dollars per 2 burritos or 28 dollars per 8 burritos.
criteria: Asked for the price of one
Didn’t write the 7 in for them

moments.see: Hands go up before anyone has filled a row.
moments.means: With no quiet think time, the first answer becomes everyone’s.
moments.say: Pencils first. Fill two rows on your own.
moments.evidence: Students have quiet time to think about a problem and work on it individually
criteria: Asked for work on paper before talk

moments.see: A pair adds a 1-hour row before filling anything else.
moments.means: A real strategy, and the one IM says to share first. The class discussion starts here.
moments.say: Keep going. You’ll share first: how you got this row.
moments.dont: Steer them to the 6 or call their way slow.
moments.evidence: Other students may be inclined to create a different table—such as the ones below—as an intermediate step for completing the given table. If so, consider asking them to share first during whole-class discussion.
criteria: Treated the 1-hour row as a real strategy
Asked them to be ready to share their first row first

moments.see: A student stares at the table: hours and 6s filled, bracelets blank.
moments.means: The structure of the table isn’t visible to them yet.
moments.say: Look back at the burrito table. What did the 7 do?
moments.dont: Fill the first row for them.
moments.evidence: For some students, the structure of the information in the table may not be apparent. Encourage them to refer to the tables in the preceding activity and think about the relationship between the ratios and unit rates there.
criteria: Sent them back to the burrito table
Asked what the unit rate did there
Didn’t fill a row for them

moments.see: On desks: 1-hour rows, row-to-row doubling, and times 6 across.
moments.means: IM’s order runs from the 1-hour row to using the 6 across the columns, so the short way grows out of the long one.
moments.say: Start us off. How did you get your first row?
moments.dont: Let the fastest pair go first.
moments.evidence: Start with students using less efficient strategies, such as those that worked out the 1 rows. Progress toward using the given unit rate to navigate from column to column in efficient ways
criteria: Ended on multiplying and dividing by 6 across
Didn’t let the fastest pair go first

moments.see: A student points from one column to the other: “You just do 6.”
moments.means: The idea is there. The words for it, times 6 one way and divide by 6 back, aren’t yet.

emerging.say: Show me. How do you go across? And back?
emerging.move: They point from hours to bracelets and back, and say or write what they did each way. Home language is fine.
emerging.nonverbal: Draw an arrow each way between the hours and bracelets columns, with a blank above each for them to fill.

developing.say: How do you go across? And back? Finish the frame.
developing.move: With “To get bracelets, I ___ the hours by ___. To get hours, I ___ the bracelets by ___,” they tell a partner, then write it on their poster. Home language first is fine.

expanding.say: How do you go across the table? And back?
expanding.move: They explain both directions on their poster in their own words, hear a classmate’s version, and make theirs clearer once. They can plan it in their home language.

criteria: Asked every level the same question: across and back
Matched the way in to the student’s level
Didn’t say the sentence for them

moments.see: For 100 bracelets a student writes “16 r 4 hours.”
moments.means: Not wrong, unfinished. 16 hours make 96 bracelets; the 4 left are 4 of the 6 made in an hour, so 4/6 = 2/3 of an hour: 16 2/3 hours.
moments.say: 4 bracelets left over. What part of an hour is that?

moments.see: A group argues over which one is the right answer.
moments.means: Each rate doesn’t belong for a different reason. There is no single answer.
moments.say: Find a reason for each one.
moments.dont: Name the one you had in mind.
moments.evidence: Typically, each of the four options “doesn’t belong” for a different reason

moments.see: A student doubles 4 pounds to 8, then is stuck at 7.
moments.means: Row-to-row multiplying runs out when 7 isn’t a multiple of 4. IM chose the numbers for that.
moments.evidence: None of the given numbers are multiples of each other from row to row (for example, 7 isn't a multiple of 4), so this problem lends itself to reasoning about unit rates.

patterns.says: “14 per 2” in the unit price column.
patterns.why: “Per burrito” is read as per order.
patterns.shows: They can keep a ratio together. Per 1 is the new step.
patterns.evidence: Students may not realize that the third column asks for dollars per 1 burrito

patterns.why: They see the third column never changes.
patterns.shows: The idea of 7.2: equivalent ratios share one unit rate.
patterns.evidence: No matter how many burritos you buy, it costs $7 per burrito.

patterns.says: A 1-hour row, then the rest from it.
patterns.why: Row-to-row reasoning is what they know.
patterns.shows: They know a unit rate means per 1.
patterns.evidence: This intermediate strategy makes good use of the “1” rows in the table

patterns.why: They use the given rate as the factor between columns.
patterns.shows: The lesson’s new idea, in their words.
patterns.evidence: multiplying the time in hours by 6 to find number of bracelets

patterns.why: They divided by the rate but left the remainder as bracelets, not part of an hour.
patterns.shows: The right move. The last step is turning 4 bracelets into 2/3 of an hour.

patterns.why: They found the other unit rate.
patterns.shows: Both unit rates, and when each is useful.
patterns.evidence: multiplying the number of bracelets by \(\frac16\) to find time in hours

patterns.why: The idea is ahead of the words.
patterns.shows: They see the factor across the columns.

predict.context: After the burrito table, pairs get a bracelet table with the speed already filled in: 6 bracelets per hour in every row. They complete it, write how they did it, then use the same strategy on a half-empty burrito table.
predict.question: How will most pairs fill the bracelet table?
predict.countQuestion: How many pairs will use the 6 directly, without building a 1-hour row?
predict.tell: If few do, the 6 in the table didn’t read as a tool. That is why the class discussion starts with the 1-hour row and builds to it: the fifth moment you’ll rehearse.

emerging.entry: When pairs walk around to look at the posters, they point to where another poster goes across the table and back, and say or write what it does each way. Home language is fine.

developing.entry: They tell a classmate how another poster goes across the table and back, and whether theirs does the same. Home language first is fine.
developing.frame: They multiplied the ___ by ___ and divided the ___ by ___. We did it the same way / a different way.

expanding.entry: They compare another poster with theirs aloud: how each goes across the table and back, and is the outcome the same? They can plan it in their home language.
expanding.frame: This poster goes across by ___ and back by ___. Ours goes across by ___ and back by ___. Both get ___.

cuts.note: Optional, with no new mathematics. Cut it first, and give its 10 minutes to 7.3.
Keep it short: one reason for each rate, then move on.

IM gives 7.3 10 minutes, with 3–4 of them quiet work. Posters and a walk-around to look at them won’t fit too. Use the minutes from 7.4, put only the bracelet table on the poster, and keep the walk-around to about 3 minutes.

neverCut: Quiet think time before partners talk, in 7.2 and 7.3
The strategy sentence under the bracelet table
Using the strategy again on the burrito table
The class discussion in IM’s order, 1-hour row first

inClass.launch: “Fill the table, then write how you did it.”
sequence: A pair who built a 1-hour row first
A pair who went row to row
A pair who multiplied by 6 across and divided 66 by 6

beforeClass: Draw the bracelet table on the board with the 6s filled in.
Put out one sheet of chart paper and a marker per pair, for the posters.
Know the answers: 12, 30, 42 bracelets; 11 and 16 2/3 hours; 2 and 4 burritos; $35 and $70.
